# Agentic Pipeline Report: 20 Newsgroups (4 categories)

## 1. Data overview

I first used `load_dataset_tool` to load four categories of the 20 Newsgroups dataset (`load_dataset_1`), which gave 2,257 documents in total. soc.religion.christian has 599 documents, sci.med 594, comp.graphics 584, and alt.atheism 480, so the classes are slightly uneven but not seriously imbalanced. When I inspected the first five rows (`inspect_data_2`), I found that the first 100 characters of every document are email headers such as From, Subject, and Organization, not the actual post. This suggests that header words may interfere with the later term analysis. The quality checks found no missing texts (`check_missing_3`) and no duplicates (`check_duplicates_4`), so no cleaning was needed. Text length, however, varies a lot (`describe_data_5`). The average document has 1,993 characters, but the median is only 1,235, the standard deviation is 3,548, and the longest document reaches 60,713. Since the mean is much higher than the median, the distribution is right-skewed: most documents are fairly short, and a few very long ones pull the average up. The categories also differ. comp.graphics has the shortest median (883) but the largest standard deviation (4,685) and the longest document, while soc.religion.christian has the longest median (1,649) and the smallest standard deviation (2,080), so its lengths are the most consistent. The box plot below shows many long outliers in every category, especially sci.med. These long documents may strongly affect the term-frequency and dimension-reduction results in later steps.

## 2. Document-term matrix and variance filtering

Next, I built the document-term matrix with `build_dtm_tool` (`build_dtm_6`), removing English stop words so the results could be compared with the Master notebook. The matrix has 35,482 terms, 258,503 non-zero entries, and a sparsity of 99.68%, all matching the Master notebook. The vocabulary begins with number strings such as 00, 000, and 0000001200, which probably come from phone numbers or IDs rather than real content, showing that the raw text still contains noise. I then applied `variance_filter_tool` with a threshold of 0.01 (`variance_filter_7`), which reduced the vocabulary from 35,482 to 5,089 terms, removing about 86%, again matching Master Question 5. The bar chart below shows the 20 terms with the highest variance. Most of them fall into three topics: graphics (jpeg, image, graphics, gif), religion (god, jesus, atheists), and medicine (hiv, health, cancer), so the remaining terms already reflect the dataset's topics. However, edu and com, which come from email addresses, also rank in the top five, showing that header noise survives this filter. In addition, jpeg has a variance of about 25, far above the rest, and the values level off after the top seven terms. I suspect a few documents repeat jpeg many times, which links back to the extremely long documents found earlier.

![Top 20 terms by variance](../plots/黃品鑫_agentic-pipeline_plot_turn44.png)

## 3. Pearson vs. Spearman correlation (target: comp.graphics)

To find terms that distinguish comp.graphics from the other categories, I ran `pearson_filter_tool` (`pearson_filter_8`) and `spearman_filter_tool` (`spearman_filter_9`) with comp.graphics as the target class. In the Pearson result, the top terms include thanks, writes, keywords, looking, vga, video, people, card, hi, and host, with writes and people negatively correlated, while graphics itself, which I expected to be the most representative term, ranks only 13th (r ≈ 0.18). Words like thanks, hi, and looking suggest that many comp.graphics posts are questions asking for technical help, while keywords, nntp, and host come from email and newsgroup headers, showing that Pearson is also affected by non-content information. The negative terms, such as writes, people, and say, are more common in the religion groups, where users often quote each other ("someone writes:") and debate opinions, and rutgers likely appears because soc.religion.christian is moderated through a rutgers.edu address. The Spearman result is clearly different: graphics ranks first with r ≈ 0.52, followed by people, files, image, god, 3d, program, thanks, file, and windows, with people and god negatively correlated. These terms relate more directly to the topic, and the header terms from the Pearson list no longer appear. I believe this difference comes from how the two coefficients are calculated. Pearson measures the linear relationship of raw counts, so it is easily pulled by a few documents with very high term counts, while Spearman first converts the values into ranks, which reduces the effect of these extreme counts. In such sparse text data, Spearman therefore reflects whether a term appears across many documents rather than how many times it repeats in a single document. Both top-10 lists match Master Question 6, which shows that my tools, called by the agent, reproduce the Master results, while the two methods still highlight different terms whose causes need explaining.

## 4. Frequent pattern mining

Next, I used `mine_patterns_tool` to run FP-Growth on the comp.graphics category (`mine_patterns_10`), with variance-filtered terms and a minimum support count of 14. It found 783 frequent patterns. The most frequent one, organization, appears in 560 of the 584 comp.graphics documents. However, this word comes from the email header, not from the graphics topic. Other frequent terms, such as tin and newsreader, are names of newsreader software, so headers still dominate the results. I then asked the agent to exclude these header terms and list the top 10 patterns with two or more terms. The top pattern is greatly + appreciated (support 25), a phrase people use when asking for help. This matches thanks ranking highly in the Pearson analysis and shows that comp.graphics posts have a clear help-seeking style, not just technical vocabulary. Other patterns, such as philosophical + significance (18) and herringshaw + tdawson (17), likely come from fixed signatures or names, and pl8 and pl9 are probably software version numbers. So even without the headers, fixed-format text still shapes the patterns. This step also revealed two problems with the agent. First, its initial answer did not fully follow my exclusion request, and it only corrected itself afterward. Second, I asked why highly relevant words like image and graphics were missing. The agent correctly explained that the variance filter keeps only terms between the 5th and 95th percentiles of variance, but its reason, that image appears in almost every document, was wrong. A term that appears exactly once in every document would have a variance of 0. The real reason is that image is distributed very unevenly: it appears zero times or once in most documents but many times in a few long ones, which puts its variance in the top 5%. This showed me that the agent's explanations are not always correct, so I still need to check them against earlier steps and the actual data.

## 5. Dimension reduction and conclusion

Finally, I used `reduce_dimensions_tool` to project the documents into two dimensions with PCA (`reduce_dimensions_11`) and t-SNE (`reduce_dimensions_12`), and both results match Master Question 9. In the PCA plot, most documents are crowded near the origin and the four categories overlap heavily. Only a few comp.graphics points lie far away, and I suspect these are the extremely long documents found earlier, whose high term counts push them to extreme positions. The two components together explain only about 21.6% of the variance (14.75% and 6.88%), so a 2D PCA cannot capture most of the differences in this high-dimensional data. In contrast, t-SNE reveals clearer local groups. alt.atheism sits in the upper left with soc.religion.christian right next to it, comp.graphics lies mostly in the lower middle, and sci.med forms a small tight cluster on the far left while the rest of it spreads across the lower half. The two religion groups stay close together, likely because they share religious vocabulary, and they separate fairly well from the other two. However, comp.graphics and sci.med still overlap considerably, and t-SNE positions should not be read as exact semantic distances, so the plot needs careful interpretation. Looking back at the whole pipeline, two problems appeared again and again. The first is email headers, which produced noise terms such as edu, com, keywords, nntp, and organization. The second is a few extremely long documents, which skewed the length statistics, pulled the Pearson correlations, and stretched the PCA axes. To improve the analysis, I would remove the headers before building the document-term matrix and use TF-IDF or length normalization to reduce the influence of very long documents.
